one_liner: Tiny hobby AT&T x86-64 to ELF assembler for C compiler output; README says often faster than GNU as, no numbers.
what_it_does: minias is a single command-line program (about 2,200 lines of C in main.c, parse.c and util.c plus a 2,780-line PEG grammar) that turns AT&T-syntax x86-64 assembly into an ELF64 relocatable object. It targets the output of GCC, Clang, cproc/QBE and chibicc and has assembled the sqlite3 amalgamation, a libc and itself. Usage is 'minias [-r iter] [-o out] [input]', reading stdin and writing stdout by default; it is not a library and does not take GNU as options.
how_it_is_fast: It does little work: the parser is generated by the vendored Minipeg (derived from Ian Piumarta's peg/leg), the whole file is parsed once into a linked list of interned statement values (a 4,096-entry direct-mapped cache built on murmurhash64a), and it then encodes instructions directly with REX/ModRM/SIB helpers and writes the ELF file. It never frees memory, keeps state in globals, and runs a fixed number of jump-relaxation passes (one by default) using worst-case label offsets instead of iterating to a fixed point. The author says the parser is the bottleneck; no profile or timing is published.
when_to_use: Bootstrapping or teaching a small C toolchain (cproc/QBE, chibicc) where a readable, hackable assembler matters more than full GNU as compatibility.
Assembling plain C compiler output (-S without -g) for x86-64 Linux ELF objects, piped as 'cc -S -O2 file.c -o - | minias -o file.o -'.
As a reference implementation of x86-64 instruction encoding and ELF relocatable output that fits in a few files under the ISC licence.
When you want to measure for yourself whether a minimal assembler shortens build time on very large generated .s files; no published numbers exist to rely on.
when_not_to_use: C++ compiler output: the grammar has no COMDAT group sections ('axG',...,comdat) and no TLS relocation suffixes (@tpoff, @gottpoff, @tlsgd), so inline functions, templates and thread_local fail to assemble.
Code that needs unwinding or debug info: .cfi_* directives are silently discarded (no .eh_frame is produced), and -g output fails because .loc and .uleb128 are not in the grammar.

AVX, AVX2 or AVX-512 code: the grammar has SSE (xmm) forms but no ymm/zmm or VEX/EVEX instructions, so -mavx2 or -march=native output fails; the roadmap item to test every opcode variant is still open.
As a drop-in 'as' behind gcc or clang: any '--' option such as gcc's '--64' prints usage and exits, so a wrapper script is needed.
Anywhere a speed claim must be backed: the only evidence is one README sentence with no workload, versions or machine.

integration.dependencies: none at run time beyond libc; build needs a C compiler, make and the vendored Minipeg generator (vendor/minipeg/minipeg.c, MIT-style licence) to produce asm_parser.c
integration.min_toolchain: not documented; a C compiler with <elf.h> and _GNU_SOURCE (Linux glibc or musl headers). The Makefile adds no -O flag; the README's manual build uses cc -O2
integration.platforms: emits x86-64 ELF64 relocatable objects only (AT&T syntax); host must provide <elf.h>
integration.thread_safety: single-threaded command-line tool with global state; not designed for in-process reuse
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — accepts a practical subset of GNU as AT&T syntax and emits compatible ELF objects, but rejects GNU as command-line options and lacks COMDAT, TLS, AVX, DWARF and unwind-table support

gotchas: Silently ignored directives: .cfi_*, .file, .ident, .type and .size parse to no-ops, so objects have no .eh_frame unwind tables and symbols are emitted without a function/object type or size (only .comm symbols get STT_OBJECT). Exceptions or backtraces through these frames, and tools that rely on symbol sizes, are affected without any error.
Unsupported syntax fails loudly ('syntax error' at a line number) rather than misassembling, so trial builds show quickly whether a codebase fits the supported subset.

Jump relaxation runs one extra pass by default using worst-case offsets; output is correct but may keep long jumps that more passes would shorten (raise with -r iter). '-r' given as the last argument with no value passes NULL to atoi and crashes.

The speed sentence ('often better than gnu as and much better than the clang assembler') dates from the 2021 README, when the parser was generated by peg/leg; it was carried unchanged through the May 2026 switches to PackCC and then Minipeg, so it describes neither the current parser nor current GNU as/clang versions. test/test.sh only compares .text bytes against clang's encoding and times nothing.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick minias over aron (Mach-O, macOS as baseline) when you need Linux ELF objects, and over Asmc, JWasm or UASM when your input is AT&T-syntax compiler output rather than MASM source; unlike Keystone it is a standalone program, not an embeddable library.
verified_claims_summary: No measurement exists: the README states that minias's performance is 'often better than gnu as and much better than the clang assembler', with no input files, timings, versions, build flags or hardware, and the repository contains no benchmark script; an independent search found no third-party numbers either.
status_note: Active hobby project (last commit 2026-06-24, 231 stars, 16 forks, ISC licence, no issues filed) and small enough to vendor, but its speed claim is directional only and it covers C compiler output rather than general C++ or SIMD-heavy code.
sources_read: WebSearch: minias x86-64 assembler andrewchambers faster than gnu as benchmark (no independent benchmark found)
